subject: English
summaryPoints: Adverbial clauses of reason can be fronted or placed clause-finally; common conjunctions include 'because', 'since', 'as', 'now that' (denoting a current causal reality), and 'as long as' (denoting causal circumstance).
Verbs differ strictly in their non-finite complementation: Group A verbs take gerunds only (admit, anticipate, avoid, consider, delay, deny, enjoy, finish, imagine, postpone, practice, suggest).
Group B verbs take to-infinitives only (afford, agree, aim, decide, demand, fail, hesitate, hope, learn, manage, offer, plan, prepare, promise, refuse, threaten, volunteer).

Group C verbs take either gerunds or to-infinitives with distinct semantic contrasts: 'remember/forget to do' (future/duty orientation) vs 'remember/forget doing' (retrospective memory); 'stop to do' (interrupt an action in order to do another) vs 'stop doing' (terminate the activity); 'try to do' (make an effort) vs 'try doing' (experiment with a method); and 'regret to say' (reluctant announcement) vs 'regret doing' (sorrow over past action).

Participle phrases function as verbal adjectives: present participles (V-ing) denote active simultaneous actions; past participles (V-ed/en) express passive states or completed conditions; and perfect participles ('having + V3') highlight an active action concluded prior to the main clause.

The process approach to writing progresses through recursive stages: prewriting (brainstorming, clustering, outlining), drafting (composing rough initial texts), revising (reorganizing content, refining thesis and supporting paragraphs), and editing (proofreading mechanics, spelling, and grammar).

formulas.label: Verbal Complementation Group A (Gerund Only)
formulas.expr: Subject + Verb(admit, avoid, deny, enjoy, finish, postpone, suggest) + V-ing(gerund) + Object

formulas.label: Verbal Complementation Group B (Infinitive Only)
formulas.expr: Subject + Verb(afford, agree, decide, fail, hope, manage, promise, refuse) + to + V1(infinitive)

formulas.label: Semantic Contrast: Remember / Stop
formulas.expr: stop + to + V1 = pause in order to act  |  stop + V-ing = terminate activity  |  remember + to + V1 = not forget duty  |  remember + V-ing = recall past memory

formulas.label: Perfect Participle Clause Formula
formulas.expr: Having + V3(past participle) + , + Subject + V2(main clause)  [Indicates earlier completed action]

examTip: Pay careful attention to verbs whose meaning changes depending on whether they take a gerund or an infinitive: 'He stopped smoking' means he quit the habit entirely, while 'He stopped to smoke' means he paused whatever he was doing in order to have a cigarette. For participle phrases, make sure the subject of the main clause matches the implied subject of the participle to prevent dangling participles.

keyDefinitions.definition: A non-finite verbal noun formed by adding '-ing' to the base verb, functioning syntactically as a subject, object, or complement.
The base form of a verb, preceded by the particle 'to' (to-infinitive) or standing alone (bare infinitive), functioning as a noun, adjective, or adverb.
A non-finite participial construction formed with 'having' plus a past participle, expressing an action that took place prior to the action of the main finite clause.
A grammatical fault where a participial phrase has no clear, syntactically present noun or pronoun to modify in the main clause.

eueeFocusTopics: Meaning-shifting verbs with gerund vs infinitive ('remember', 'stop', 'regret', 'try')
Participial phrase modifiers (present, past, and perfect participle clauses)
Phrasal verbs based on 'make' ('make up for', 'make off with', 'make for')
